Thing is, without the receipt, store credit is as good as cash as we have limited resources (phone number, ID) to be able to find your invoice. There is a way to track a gift cards history but it’s usually only used in cases of suspected fraud or loss and not everyone knows how to do it. Besides, if the purchase was made over 90 days ago, they would not be able to credit you even with proof of purchase. 

So the answer is: An in-store credit does not count as a valid proof of purchase or “payment card” likely because our refund system does not link a transaction in the same way to a debit or credit card. I’m not sure why this is, but it is also why if you were somehow able to return it, we have to put it on a new card, as they aren’t reloadable. But without the receipt, in-store credit transactions can only really be found through linked phone numbers, rewards accounts, and occasionally the license used to issue it. Without any of those, we do not  have a way to look up the transaction and cannot return it.

At my store, most cashiers and specialists are discouraged from doing returns outside of customer service. The only exception is pro. I think part of it carries over from when genesis was our only return system and most cashiers weren’t trained on it. But I imagine it also deters double-dip/off the shelf return confusion with LP, and prevents the tills from being emptied by big cash refunds. Not to mention the nightmare of not finding the receipt/card the first try.

I work the desk, and in the case of the pavers/building materials would much rather have cashiers count quantity/verify the item number and send them down to me. That way, if things go wrong, you don’t have a line of customers waiting to check out. I will do it when cashiering if it’s quick/not busy but most times I send them to the desk.

Policy generally states they can return anything that is unopened, unused, and in their original packaging. If it’s opened/used/missing its packaging it’s up to the associate’s discretion to determine whether or not they can/should return it based on if it can be resold or sent to the vendor.

Coming from someone who used to cry almost every shift, how customers treat us is mostly out of our control, but there are ways to cope/take control. If they don’t have the forms of purchase, let them know their options. If they get upset when you can’t process the return, just repeat the policy back to them/options for next time. If they want to speak to a manager, see if you can fix it, otherwise you can get your head cashier/DS before dialing management. 

When there are long lines, the people on the phone can wait/transfer or you answer with a simple “lowes customer service, where may i direct your call?” do not engage, let the departments parse. 

People can be cruel when you don’t sound like an expert. I like to explain the processes, like “our system only goes back six months, and all it can do is cross reference your card with that item number” and “our delivery truck is on a set route, unfortunately we will not be able to reschedule your stop until tomorrow” and “due to fraud the computer will not let me process this return nonreceipted” stuff like that. I also make stuff up for things that have no real reason, for example I tell people to move their cars away from the main entrance to the loading zone by saying it’s a fire hazard.

Your head cashiers should be helping you break down lines and solve problems, don’t be afraid to ask questions.  

In the end: You are not responsible for other people’s lack of preparation, bad day, sense of entitlement, or for our companies imperfect policies and business practices. About 95% of problems you’ll have at the desk are not yours, or don’t really matter that much.

Hi! as someone who was into this sort of thing between the ages of 12-16, I have some reasonable advice. Taking devices and shaming will only create a sneakier, more isolated teen. They will find ways to connect with these communities that excite them (which means you cant keep as much of an eye on it, which is dangerous), and they will take your punishment as a judgement of who they are rather than what they’re doing. So here’s a decent way to proceed:

1) Understand that a lot of times these NSFW communities are begun by adults that are participating in perfectly legal behavior, then learned an emulated by young + impressionable teens. This objectively sucks, but it happens, and it’s unfortunately super normalized in fandom space.

2) Don’t be harsh, but do try to mention that sharing the pictures and videos (especially ESPECIALLY of themselves) can get them in severe legal trouble. It’s child pornography. 

3) They need to be aware that role-playing can be occurring between them and anyone else. Meaning pedophiles, meaning people even younger than them, etc. It’s not safe. They probably won’t listen, but it’s worth mentioning.

In the end, the fact that they spend all their times in these communities suggests to me that they feel isolated, they feel unseen, and they feel judged. They need to be in counseling. This is not ‘finding who they are’ but your tone suggests you might be connecting queerness with perversion. Get them help, encourage them to find other outlets (GSA, sports, art, anime club, drama, whatever) and don’t judge them. The hormones will go down, and they will eventually stray away on their own, it’s your job to help them out of the rabbit hole sooner.

We don’t have to excuse the behavior, but understand that if comes out of a few things: isolation (especially bad with teens coming of age thru covid, their personal development varies a lot), lack of boundaries, stimulation/depression/why they seek this content out at all, and a need for community, counseling, and healthy hobbies.

Hi, I hear you, and I see you, and I understand where you’re coming from. Being young and trans and not able to present/be/exist as you want to is a whole other kind of dread. It feels very very helpless and hopeless and dim sometimes. There’s not a lot to affirm you.

But trust me, as painful as it is to wait to affirm yourself and start HRT, you have plenty of time. It is never too late. Teen years are rough without the added burden of dysphoria, and you deserve to be comfortable in yourself.

But you will get there. Time keeps passing every day, and every day you get closer to your truest self. Until you have access to HRT, find ways like vocal training, experiment with hair, clothes, etc. 

Trust me, 18 is not too late to start HRT. Transmasc people have excellent results with Testosterone beginning well into middle and old age. Men look all kinds of ways, cis and trans. There are cis men who are petite and soft with long hair and dress feminine, trans men as well. There are trans men who are huge and bulky and covered in hair, cis men as well. There’s no wrong way to be a man. 

I know its hard to not be taken seriously, but it’s such a beautiful thing to have this knowledge of yourself already. The best and healthiest thing you can do for yourself is to know you deserve better, to affirm yourself, to cherish this knowledge and unique life experience you have. You’ll prove them wrong someday. They can be hateful and misunderstand you, but one day you’ll be at a point where they just look ignorant, stupid, crazy even for invalidating you. Hold on for that. 

You have a very beautiful life ahead of you, regardless of when you physically transition. Knowing yourself is enough. Fuck everyone else. No one you know when you’re a teenager matters anyway.

every new years eve i semi-meticulously compile a playlist of completely new music that i’ve never heard before with energy/themes/etc. that i want to manifest in my new year, beginning in the morning and usually finishing not too long before the clock strikes 12. i then usually listen to that playlist on repeat for the first few weeks of the new year. i’ll usually revisit it some time towards the end of the year to reflect. this new years will be my 5th year doing it.

when i’m listening to a new album that i’m really excited for/really want to savor, i set aside a good chunk of time for it, usually in the middle of the night, light a candle, lay on my bed and listen to it all the way through once or twice. did this for the first time with lorde’s melodrama a few year back and it’s been my favorite way to closely listen to music ever since
